idiom_name: ops struct of function pointers in a header plus an opaque handle (hand-built vtable)
implementation_notes: C has no classes, so the contract is hand-written: a struct whose members are function pointers, declared in a public header, with the object passed back to every operation as its first argument (the self convention). The struct holds no data beyond the operations - state lives in the concrete object the callbacks receive - which makes the stateless contract the natural C form, and the Linux kernel's *_operations / *_ops structs (file_operations and friends) are its canonical use. What replaces the classic structure is that header plus a forward-declared, opaque handle type: clients see the operations and never the representation. GLib's registered GInterface is the heavyweight alternative, worth its type registration, prerequisites and per-type interface_init wiring only when the contract has to be discovered or combined at run time.
pitfalls: The ops struct is not the object: if an operation forgets its self parameter the contract silently binds to one global implementation.
A missing initialiser leaves a NULL function pointer that traps only when that operation is called - fill the whole struct (C99 designated initialisers) and validate it once at construction.
If the handle is not opaque (the struct is defined in the header), clients reach into the representation and the contract stops being their only dependency.
Function-pointer tables carry no versioning: adding an operation changes every initialiser, so a published C contract is expensive to extend in place.
